item.title: The Original Data Company
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
“We are not a tech company.” I have heard the sentence in meetings at the insurer I work for, which since a recent merger is also a bank, and before that at a bank where I worked, said by smart, experienced people, usually as a reason: for why a platform does not need to be built in-house, why engineering is a cost to be contained, why the interesting work happens somewhere else. Every time, I am baffled, because I think the opposite is true. An insurer is not a financial company that happens to use technology. It is a technology company that happens to hold a balance sheet, and in a precise sense it is the oldest data company there is.

This post is the argument for that. It builds on The River and the Canal, which ended with the observation that banks and insurers sell sameness, and on a note about why trust is earned by sameness. It is not a post about monetary politics, although it starts with money, because money is where the abstraction begins.

Abstract businesses

You cannot touch an insurance policy. You cannot touch a bank account either, or a pension, or a share in a fund. What these businesses sell is abstract: a promise that something will happen in a certain way when certain conditions are met. A large part of the economy, most of what economists call the service sector, works like this, even when it does not look alike from the outside. A bank, an insurer, a broker, a payment provider and a land registry have different products and the same substance. They sell kept promises.

Money itself is the deepest example. The textbook story says that people bartered until someone invented coins, and that credit came later. David Graeber’s Debt: The First 5,000 Years takes that story apart: “In fact, our standard account of monetary history is precisely backwards. We did not begin with barter, discover money, and then eventually develop credit systems. It happened precisely the other way around. What we now call virtual money came first.” Credit systems, ways of keeping account of who owes what to whom, are documented in Mesopotamia thousands of years before coinage appeared, between roughly 600 and 500 BCE. Money, in that reading, started as a record of trust, and it still is one. A currency is worth what people believe it is worth, which is why the more accurate word for it is the old one, credit, from the Latin credere, to believe.

How that record is created today is less mysterious than it sounds, and less public than most people assume. In 2014 the Bank of England published a short article in its Quarterly Bulletin, “Money creation in the modern economy”, explaining that most money in a modern economy takes the form of bank deposits, and that the principal way those deposits are created is commercial banks making loans. The Swiss economist Mathias Binswanger built a whole book on the consequences, Geld aus dem Nichts (Money Out of Nothing, 2015). Its first chapter, on how commercial banks create money, opens under a heading that says it all: “the false idea of banks as financial intermediaries” (“Die falsche Vorstellung von Banken als Finanzintermediäre”). The journalist Paul Schreyer takes the argument further in Wer regiert das Geld? (Who Governs Money?, 2016):

All the decision-making power and sovereignty of a society comes down to two simple questions: Who may create money? And who decides how it is used?

Alle Entscheidungsgewalt und Souveränität einer Gesellschaft läuft auf zwei simple Fragen hinaus: Wer darf das Geld erschaffen? Und wer entscheidet über seine Verwendung?

There is a large and heated debate about what this means for states and democracies, and I find it important, but it is not the subject here. The point I need is simpler: even the most basic product of the financial industry is an abstraction, a carefully maintained record of trust.

What these businesses are for

Nobody wrote a mandate for banks and insurers, and yet they fulfil one. Every society has to answer two questions, again and again, and it has never managed to answer them without institutions. Where should its resources go? And who carries the cost when something goes wrong that nobody could have foreseen? Economists have names for the two functions. The first is capital allocation, or financial intermediation: deciding which of all the possible futures gets funded. The second is risk pooling, or mutualisation: spreading the cost of misfortunes that strike a few across the many who might have been struck. Banks do the first, insurers the second. Both look as if they had been designed by the collective body we call humanity, and in a sense they were, slowly, by trial and error, over centuries.

Joseph Schumpeter saw the first function more clearly than anyone. In The Theory of Economic Development he describes the banker not as a middleman who passes on other people’s savings but as the one who decides which new ventures happen at all: “He makes possible the carrying out of new combinations, authorises people, in the name of society as it were, to form them. He is the ephor of the exchange economy.” An ephor was a magistrate in ancient Sparta. Schumpeter’s point is that by deciding whom to lend to, banks decide, on society’s behalf, what gets built and how a civilisation grows.

The second function is just as old and just as social. Before there were insurers, there were families and clans that absorbed the loss when one member’s house burned down, guilds that supported members who fell ill, villages with common funds for fire and flood. Taleb, in Skin in the Game, calls that kind of in-group protection a form of self-insurance, “something that can only work for a limited number of people and can’t be universalized”. An insurer is what you get when it is universalised: the same thing done with strangers, at scale, under contract: everyone pays a little so that nobody has to pay everything. Social insurance does it through the state. The principle underneath is the same in all of them, a kind of solidarity made calculable.

Both functions are fractal, which by now will surprise nobody who has read Everything is a fractal. A person decides where to put their time, attention and money. A family decides which child goes to which school and who takes over the farm. A tribe decides who hunts and who stays. A company decides which products to fund, a bank which companies, a society which industries. At every scale it is the same act: placing bets on the future with limited resources, and sharing the losses of the bets that fail.

And at every scale the bet needs someone willing to take the other side. When Christopher Columbus wanted to sail west across an ocean whose far side nobody in Europe could chart, he spent years looking for backers, until the Crown of Castile agreed, persuaded and helped by Luis de Santángel, a royal finance official who arranged much of the money. That is Knight’s uncertainty in its purest form: no table of similar voyages, no measurable odds, only judgement and a willingness to lose. Somebody chose to take the bet. Every bank loan to a new venture is a smaller version of that choice.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb has spent a series of books on what happens at the edges of these functions. The Black Swan is about events defined by “rarity, extreme impact, and retrospective (though not prospective) predictability”, which is exactly where lending and insurance fail most painfully. Taleb is unusually kind to one part of the industry. Reinsurers, who carry the catastrophe risks that primary insurers pass on, are in his account, “unlike bankers”, “introspective enough to know that it actually could have been far worse, because the past twenty years did not have a big catastrophe, and all you need is one of those per century to kiss the business good-bye.” Skin in the Game starts from the code of Hammurabi, which punished a builder whose house collapsed on its owner, because “the best place to hide risks is “in the corners,” in burying vulnerabilities to rare events that only the architect (or the trader) can detect.” Insurance has a famous example of the opposite: for most of its history, the individual members who backed policies at Lloyd’s, the Names, were liable with everything they owned. And Antifragile draws the distinction that matters most for an institution whose job is to absorb other people’s shocks: “The resilient resists shocks and stays the same; the antifragile gets better.”

The point for this argument is what all of these functions have in common. Whether it is a banker choosing a borrower, an underwriter pricing a ship, or a reinsurer pricing a hurricane, the work is the same: assessing the world, putting numbers on it, and deciding which promise to make to whom at what price. Society delegated two of its most important decisions to institutions whose core activity is calculation. That is the next step in the argument.

What technology actually is

If the product is a record of trust, what does it take to produce one well? Mostly, it takes doing the same thing every time. In the trust note I described the two halves of that: consistency, the same input giving the same outcome over time, and integrity, the thing being whole and being what it claims to be. A bank that books your payment differently depending on the clerk, or an insurer whose policy means something different from what its documents say, has nothing left to sell.

That is also my working definition of technology, at least the kind that matters here. Strip away the hardware, and technology is the formalisation of trust into procedure: taking something you would otherwise have to believe and turning it into something that happens the same way every time and can be checked. A ledger is a technology in this sense, so is double-entry bookkeeping, so is a database transaction, and so is a workflow engine. In The River and the Canal I described how every layer of computing made one more thing predictable so that the people above it could stop thinking about it. Financial institutions were doing that with paper, people and procedures long before computers existed, and when computers arrived, banks and insurers were among their earliest commercial users, because they were already in the business computers are for.

So my claim is that abstract businesses always were technology companies, rather than that they should become them, and that the sentence “we are not a tech company” is a misunderstanding of their own product. Of all of them, the insurer is the clearest case.

Bitcoin, or trust without an institution

If technology is formalised trust and money is a record of trust, then sooner or later someone was going to try to formalise money itself, all the way down, until no institution was left. On 31 October 2008, six weeks after Lehman Brothers collapsed and exactly eighteen years before I started writing this post, someone calling themselves Satoshi Nakamoto sent a short message titled “Bitcoin P2P e-cash paper” to a mailing list for cryptographers. The paper it linked, “Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System”, states its aim in its first sentence: “A purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution.” A few paragraphs later it names what it wants to replace: “What is needed is an electronic payment system based on cryptographic proof instead of trust.” When the network started in January 2009, its very first block carried a line from that day’s front page of The Times: “Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.”

That is why Bitcoin, and the wider idea of a distributed ledger or blockchain that it introduced, caused the fuss it did. It went straight at the heart of what abstract financial institutions do. Banks keep the ledger of who owes what, which Graeber shows is the oldest form of money there is. Central banks and, as the Bank of England explains, commercial banks decide how much money exists. Bitcoin replaced the first with a public ledger that every participant can check and nobody can quietly rewrite, and the second with an algorithm: new coins appear on a fixed schedule, halving every 210,000 blocks, until the supply approaches 21 million and stops. In the terms of this post, it is my definition of technology taken to its extreme, trust formalised so completely that the trusted institution is no longer needed. It is also the purest answer anyone has given to Schreyer’s first question, who may create money: nobody, only the protocol.

What happened next is just as instructive. Within a few years an industry of exchanges, custodians and brokers grew up around the protocol, because most people did not want to hold their own keys, verify their own transactions or have no one to call when something went wrong. The crypto broker I mentioned in The River and the Canal sells exactly what banks sell: sameness, safekeeping, a promise. Bitcoin answered who may create money; it did not answer Schreyer’s second question, who decides how it is used, nor the questions of what gets funded and who carries the cost of misfortune. Those functions, capital allocation and risk pooling, are still performed by institutions that crunch numbers about the world, which is the argument of this post.

And then there is the question I find hardest to let go of: who actually invented it. Satoshi Nakamoto stopped communicating publicly in the early 2010s, and the identity has never been established; a British court ruled in 2024 that one well-known claimant, Craig Wright, is not Satoshi. My own speculation, and I want to be clear that it is speculation and nothing more, is that it may have come from inside an intelligence agency, the NSA perhaps, or another one. The hints people point to are thin but real: the hash function at the core of Bitcoin, SHA-256, belongs to the SHA-2 family designed by the NSA and published as a federal standard in 2001 and 2002, and an NSA research report from 1996, “How to Make a Mint: The Cryptography of Anonymous Electronic Cash”, had studied anonymous digital money more than a decade earlier. None of that is evidence; SHA-256 was public and widely used, and the electronic cash literature was well known among cryptographers. I hold the idea the way I hold the factory under the sea: as a thought experiment worth turning over. If it were true, it would be the strangest twist of all, an institution building the tool designed to make institutions unnecessary.

The original data company

In 1693 the astronomer Edmond Halley, of the comet, published a paper in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society with a dry title: “An Estimate of the Degrees of the Mortality of Mankind”. He had been sent birth and death records from the city of Breslau, and from them he built a life table: of a group of people born in the same year, how many survive to each age. Then he did something new with it. He used the table to calculate what a life annuity should cost, how much a person of a given age should pay for an income until death. Halley’s recommendations to the English crown were ignored for decades, but the method was not. A collected dataset, a statistical model fitted to it, and a price derived from the model: that is the whole architecture of insurance, and of every data company since, written down three centuries before anyone said “big data”.

The rest of the toolkit arrived around the same time. In 1654 Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat had worked out the mathematics of chance in a correspondence about gambling. In 1713 Jacob Bernoulli’s posthumous Ars Conjectandi gave the law of large numbers, the reason an insurer can be confident about a thousand houses while knowing nothing about any single one. And in the late 1680s, in Edward Lloyd’s coffee house in London, merchants and ship owners gathered for the most valuable thing the house offered, reliable shipping news, and the people who underwrote voyages there became Lloyd’s of London. The house also gave its name to Lloyd’s List, a shipping newspaper. The first great insurance market grew up around an information service.

Frank Knight, whom I leaned on in the river essay, explains why this works. Risk, in his sense, is uncertainty you can measure across many similar cases, and measurable risk can be insured. An insurer is a machine for turning measurable risk into procedure. Its entire edge is measuring better than the next insurer.

Modelling the model

Look at what an insurer actually does all day, and translate it.

What the insurer calls itWhat a tech company would call it
Underwritingpredicting the probability and size of a loss for one customer
Pricinga model that turns that prediction into a price that holds across a portfolio
Claims handlinga high-volume workflow with fraud detection and exception handling
Reservingforecasting what is already owed but not yet known
Capital modellingsimulating the whole balance sheet under thousands of scenarios
Reinsurancebuying protection from someone who models your models
Distributiona funnel, a recommender and a customer interface

None of these rows is a metaphor. Pricing is a model fitted to data. Reserving is a forecast. Capital modelling is simulation, and regulators require it. Under the Swiss Solvency Test, for example, an insurer has to quantify its risks on its whole balance sheet every year, with a standard model or, where that does not fit its risks, an internal model of its own that the supervisor approves. Solvency II in the European Union works on the same principle. Since Hurricane Andrew in 1992, which bankrupted several insurers that had priced storms from past claims, and the Northridge earthquake two years later, property insurers have relied on catastrophe models that simulate hurricanes, earthquakes and floods across their portfolios.

And there is a fractal in it, which I cannot resist. An insurer models the world. A reinsurer, the insurer of insurers, models the insurers’ models. A regulator models the reinsurers and insurers to decide how much capital the whole system needs. Each layer is the same activity one scale up: build a model of the layer below, find where it is wrong, and put a price on the error.

   ┌────────────────────────────┐
   │ data about the world       │  claims history, exposure, weather,
   │                            │  vehicles, buildings, health
   └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                 ▼
   ┌────────────────────────────┐
   │ model                      │  probability and size of loss,
   │                            │  per customer and per portfolio
   └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                 ▼
   ┌────────────────────────────┐
   │ price and promise          │  the policy: a prediction wrapped
   │                            │  in a contract
   └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                 ▼
   ┌────────────────────────────┐
   │ procedure                  │  claims handled the same way,
   │                            │  every time, for decades
   └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                 ▼
   ┌────────────────────────────┐
   │ outcomes                   │  feed the next model
   └────────────────────────────┘

Every step in that pipeline is technology in the sense I defined: either a model that makes a prediction, or a procedure that keeps a promise the same way every time. The balance sheet sits underneath as the backstop that makes the promise credible. It is not the product.

Who sees the road

If the edge of an insurer is measuring better, then the most important question about its future is who has the best measurements. For most of history the answer was the insurer itself: it had the claims history, the actuaries and the tables. That is changing, and the clearest example is the car.

A modern car is a sensor platform that happens to have wheels. It knows how hard you brake, how fast you take corners, whether you use your seat belt and what time of night you drive. Tesla already sells insurance in parts of the United States that is priced from exactly that. Its real-time insurance computes a Safety Score from the vehicle’s own data, without any extra device, and adjusts the premium monthly according to the score and the miles driven.

George Hotz saw the same thing from a stranger angle. He became famous for jailbreaking the iPhone and the PlayStation 3, then founded comma.ai, which makes an open-source driver-assistance system that people retrofit into their cars. In interviews, including his conversation with Lex Fridman, he has floated the idea that comma’s real long-term business could be insurance: a company whose devices see how millions of miles are driven knows who is a good driver better than any insurer working from age, postcode and claims history. Whether comma ever does it matters less than the logic, which is airtight. Whoever has the best model of the risk can offer the best price for it, and the best model goes to whoever sees the road.

The same logic applies far beyond cars. Phones know how people move, watches know how they sleep and how their hearts behave, buildings increasingly know when their pipes leak. Every one of those sensors is, potentially, an underwriting model held by someone who is not an insurer. An insurer that believes it is not a tech company is a company that has not yet noticed who its real competitors are.

Banks and brokers, briefly

The argument transfers, with different nouns. A bank’s core decision, whether to lend, is a prediction: will this borrower pay back? Credit scoring, which FICO turned into a general-purpose score in the United States in 1989, is a model, and modern lenders run on far richer ones. Payments are a giant, real-time fraud-detection problem. Trading desks are models and execution engines. A broker is a matching and routing system with a promise of fair execution attached. Each of them sells a prediction or a procedure, wrapped in trust, backed by capital. The balance sheet is what makes the promise believable. The technology is what makes it true.

Why the sentence persists

If the argument is so clear, why do intelligent people in these companies keep saying “we are not a tech company”? I think there are three reasons, and none of them is stupidity.

The first is accounting. In most banks and insurers, IT grew up as a cost centre that served “the business”, and the organisation chart still reflects that. Conway’s law, which I wrote about in The River and the Canal, does the rest: a company organised as if technology were a supporting function builds systems that behave like one, which then confirms the belief.

The second is identity. “Tech company” in public imagination means Silicon Valley: consumer apps, hoodies, growth at any cost, a habit of breaking things. A Swiss insurer that has kept its promises for a century and a half does not want to be that, and it is right not to. But the fix is a better definition of technology, not a rejection of it. Keeping promises consistently for a century and a half is a technical achievement.

The third is that the technology in these companies is old enough to have become invisible. The ratchet I described in the river essay applies here too: once a layer works, nobody sees it any more. Nobody in an insurer marvels at the actuarial tables, the policy administration system or the claims workflow, the way nobody marvels at running water. They are simply how things are done. Marc Andreessen wrote in 2011 that software was eating the world. For insurers, it was eaten long ago and has been digesting ever since.

Why it matters now

This would be a curiosity if nothing were changing. Two things are.

The first is the sensors, as above. The data that defines risk is moving out of insurers’ hands and into cars, phones, wearables and buildings. An insurer that does not think of itself as a data company will wake up as a balance sheet that someone else’s model rents.

The second is agents. In the river essay I argued that language agents are strongest in the symbolic world, the world of documents, contracts, procedures and code, and that this is exactly where banks and insurers already live. Their products are contracts and their factories are procedures. That makes them the companies most exposed to what agents can do, and also the companies best placed to benefit, if they treat agents as a new kind of engineering and not as a new kind of vendor. An insurer that sees itself as a technology company will ask how to let agents explore its claims, its underwriting and its operations, and how to turn what they find into procedures it can trust. An insurer that sees itself as something else will buy a chatbot.

The honest counterargument

There is a real objection, and it deserves a real answer. Insurers are not only models. They hold risk capital, which no software company does. A large part of their profit comes from investing the premiums they collect before claims are paid, what Warren Buffett calls the float, money an insurer holds but does not own. They are regulated as financial institutions, and their brands are built on solidity, not on code. Surely that makes them financial companies first?

I think it makes them financial companies too, which is not the same thing. Capital is what makes the promise credible: without it, a prediction is just an opinion. The float is a consequence of the timing of the promise. Regulation exists because the promises matter so much. But none of those things is what the customer buys, and none of them decides whether one insurer beats another. Two insurers with the same capital and the same regulator win or lose on who measures risk better, prices it better and keeps the promise more consistently and more cheaply. Those are all technical problems. Buffett himself has warned that float can be drowned by poor underwriting results, which is another way of saying that the model comes first.

What changes if you accept it

If an insurer is a technology company, a few things follow, and none of them requires hoodies.

  • Own the models. Pricing, underwriting, claims triage and capital models are the product. Outsourcing them is outsourcing the business.
  • Own the data, and the context around it. Including the data about your own systems, which is the argument of IT Intelligence: a company that cannot answer questions about itself cannot build reliable technology on top of itself.
  • Treat engineers, actuaries and data scientists as one craft. They are doing the same thing with different tools: turning uncertainty into procedure.
  • Make procedures first-class. Claims and underwriting procedures are code, whether they are written down in a manual or in a workflow engine. Treat them like code: versioned, tested against past cases, replayable.
  • Go where the sensors are. Partner with the companies that see the road, the home and the body, or become one.
  • Let agents explore, and keep what works. The insurer’s oldest skill, turning measured risk into a procedure that runs the same way every time, is exactly the skill the agentic era needs.

Closing

Halley’s life table was a dataset, a model and a price. Lloyd’s was an insurance market built around a news service. Every policy since has been a prediction wrapped in a promise, and every claims department a procedure designed to keep that promise the same way, every time. That is technology in the only sense that matters for these businesses: the formalisation of trust. Insurers do not need to become tech companies. They need to notice that they already are, and that the competition for the next model of the world has already started, often in companies that do not call themselves insurers at all.

References

  • David Graeber, Debt: The First 5,000 Years, Melville House, 2011, updated and expanded edition 2014.
  • Michael McLeay, Amar Radia and Ryland Thomas, Money creation in the modern economy, Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin, 2014 Q1.
  • Mathias Binswanger, Geld aus dem Nichts: Wie Banken Wachstum ermöglichen und Krisen verursachen (Money Out of Nothing: How Banks Enable Growth and Cause Crises), Wiley-VCH, 2015; translations are mine.
  • Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, 2008, and the announcement on the cryptography mailing list, 31 October 2008.
  • The Bitcoin genesis block and its embedded Times headline.
  • SHA-2, the hash function family designed by the NSA and standardised by NIST.
  • Laurie Law, Susan Sabett and Jerry Solinas, “How to Make a Mint: The Cryptography of Anonymous Electronic Cash”, National Security Agency, 1996.
  • Paul Schreyer, Wer regiert das Geld? Banken, Demokratie und Täuschung (Who Governs Money? Banks, Democracy and Deception), Westend, 2016; translations are mine.
  • Joseph A. Schumpeter, The Theory of Economic Development, 1911, English translation 1934; the banker quote as cited in Festré and Nasica, MPRA paper 67694 from the 1983 edition, p. 74.
  • Risk pool, on pooling and mutualisation.
  • Luis de Santángel, on the financing of Columbus’s first voyage.
  • Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan (2007), Antifragile (2012) and Skin in the Game (2018).
  • Edmond Halley, An Estimate of the Degrees of the Mortality of Mankind, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 17, 1693, pp. 596 to 610.
  • Jacob Bernoulli, Ars Conjectandi, 1713.
  • Lloyd’s of London, on its origins in Edward Lloyd’s coffee house.
  • Frank H. Knight, Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit, 1921.
  • Tesla, Real-Time Insurance and the Safety Score.
  • comma.ai and the Lex Fridman podcast with George Hotz.
  • On catastrophe modelling after Hurricane Andrew: Insurance Journal, Lessons Learned from Hurricane Andrew.

  • The History of the FICO Score.
  • Marc Andreessen, “Why Software Is Eating the World”, The Wall Street Journal, 2011.
  • Warren Buffett, letters to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, on insurance float.

item.title: Learning to Play
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
This month I have been reading The Infinity Machine, Sebastian Mallaby’s biography of Demis Hassabis, the chess prodigy from North London who founded DeepMind, the laboratory behind AlphaGo and AlphaFold. I picked it up because I wanted to understand one of the early architects of the AI we now live with, told by someone who had thirty hours of his time, and because almost everything that interests me, games, simulations, the question of what a machine can learn on its own, runs through his story. A hundred pages in, there is a scene I have not been able to put down.

It is 1988 and Hassabis is twelve. He has bought a Commodore Amiga 500 with his chess winnings, and in Foyles, the big bookshop on Charing Cross Road, he finds a slim paperback: The Chess Computer Handbook by David Levy. He reads it in one sitting. Levy explains how a chess program is built from three parts. The board has to be turned into numbers. A function has to look at a position and say who is better. And a search has to try moves, and the replies to them, and the replies to those, cutting off the branches that are obviously bad because the tree grows faster than any computer can follow. Hassabis tries to build it, finds that the Amiga chokes on chess, and writes an Othello program instead, which beats his five-year-old brother.

I put the book down at that point, partly because I recognised the boy a little, and partly because I realised two things. The first is that those three parts are still the whole of a chess program. Thirty-eight years later, the strongest engines in the world are a board in numbers, an evaluation function, and a tree search with pruning; what has changed is that the evaluation function is now learned by a machine rather than written by a person, and that the machine learned it by playing against itself. The second is that the laptop on my desk has thirty thousand times the memory of that Amiga, and I had never built the three parts myself.

So I did, this month. I wrote three game engines in Rust, for chess, for Japanese shogi, and for Go, compiled them to WebAssembly so they play in a browser on my phone, and built the training loop that is supposed to make one of them stronger than I could make it by hand. The app is at kishi.raskell.io and the code is on GitHub. This is an account of why those three games, why those tools, and what happened when the ideas in the books met one ordinary machine.

The book, the man and the lab

Mallaby is not a technology writer by trade. He is a former contributing editor of the Financial Times, twice a Pulitzer finalist, now a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, and his earlier books were about money: hedge funds in More Money Than God, Alan Greenspan in The Man Who Knew, venture capital in The Power Law. That turns out to be the right background. The Infinity Machine is a biography and a company history at once, built on about thirty hours of conversation with Hassabis and more than a hundred interviews around him, and it takes the question of why someone would build a technology they believe to be dangerous as seriously as the question of how. It came out earlier this year. I am reading it slowly, and the AlphaGo chapters are still ahead of me, which I find I do not mind, because I would rather meet them with my own version of the thing running.

Hassabis, if you do not follow the field, is the person it now treats as its elder statesman, at fifty. Born in Finchley in 1976 to a Singaporean Chinese mother and a Greek Cypriot father, he was a chess master at thirteen and the second-strongest player of his age in the world. At sixteen he was co-writing Theme Park at the games studio Bullfrog, a game that sold millions. He read computer science at Cambridge, ran a games studio of his own for seven years, and then went back to university for a doctorate in neuroscience, because he thought the only way to build an intelligent machine was to understand the one existing example first. In 2010, in an attic on Russell Square, he founded DeepMind with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman, at a time when almost nobody in the field believed that what they proposed was possible. The first real money came from a Peter Thiel fund whose partners rated the science A-plus and the business model an F.

DeepMind was conceived as a Manhattan Project for artificial intelligence, and its method is what connects the book to this article. The bet was to combine two branches of the field that were both unfashionable in 2010: deep learning, the layered neural networks Geoffrey Hinton had spent a quarter of a century defending, and reinforcement learning, in which a program learns from the consequences of its own actions rather than from labelled examples, with ideas from neuroscience on top. The proving ground was games, because games have rules you can write down and scores you can read off the board. The first result, shown in 2013, was one agent that learned to play Atari games from the pixels alone. Google bought the company in 2014. In 2016 AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in Seoul, and in 2017 its successor, AlphaZero, learned chess, shogi and Go from nothing but the rules and games against itself, with one algorithm, and beat the strongest existing program at each. Those are the three games in this article, in that order, and self-play is the loop I built. AlphaFold followed in 2020, then the predicted shapes of two hundred million proteins, then the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024. Even the name is a triple nod: to deep learning, to Deep Blue, and to Deep Thought, the computer in The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy that was asked for the answer to everything.

Why am I reading it? Partly for the obvious reason: I work on AI platforms for a living and wanted the story of one of the architects of this revolution from the inside, and the book is exactly that and more. Partly because of the parallels, which kept catching me off guard: a games designer who smuggled a simulation into a theme park, a competitor who cannot pass a board game without wanting to win it, a man who thinks of the world as information and of the mind as something that builds reality rather than records it. I recognise more of that than is comfortable. And partly because of the belief. Hassabis believed in artificial intelligence when almost nobody did, with a conviction the book is honest enough to call close to religious, and he was right. There is a strand of transhumanism running through the story, from the Iain Banks novels he read at Bullfrog to the Singularity Summit where DeepMind found its first investor, and he keeps a dry British distance from the Californian version of it. I have a strand of my own, with a different spin and from a different direction, and that is a subject for another piece. It is enough to say here that I did not come to the book as a sceptic.

What hooked me in those early pages, more than the prodigy story, is how often games are the way in. Hassabis learns programming through chess. His first intelligent program plays Othello. At Cambridge he learns Go from a professor and takes shogi far enough to reach the top of the English rankings. His friend David Silver, who will later lead the AlphaGo work, finds his way into the field through a textbook on reinforcement learning, read in the south of France after their games company failed. Mallaby traces the thread back to Claude Shannon’s 1950 paper on programming a computer to play chess, which Levy’s handbook had introduced to the twelve-year-old. Shannon wrote that chess programs had no practical importance, but that mastering a game might serve as “a wedge in attacking other problems of a similar nature and of greater significance”. That sentence is seventy-six years old and still the best one-line justification I know for spending a month on board games.

My own games

My own chess is a smaller story. I joined a chess club in my early teens, played the regional tournaments, and did well in a few of them: nothing that would have sent a chess columnist across the hall to talk to my father, as one did for Hassabis when he was six, and nothing I would put in the same paragraph as his career if the book had not put the two of us in the same bookshop. But the game stayed. I do not turn down a game when one is offered; the last one was against a coworker and friend on Union Square in San Francisco, this year. I have a weakness for the big outdoor sets with knee-high pieces, and there are two I like, one in Lucerne and one beside the Rhine here in Basel. On trains I play on lichess on my phone. And I have enjoyed, more than I expected to, the odd second life the game found in the 2020s, when a television series about a fictional prodigy sent people out to buy boards and grandmasters turned into streamers with audiences no tournament hall could hold. I did not see that coming, and I am not complaining.

The other half of my gaming life is what German calls Aufbauspiele, the building games: Anno, Die Siedler, the whole tycoon genre, anything where you lay down a world with rules and watch it run. Hassabis’s Theme Park is one of them, which made that chapter feel personal. The visitors who get thirsty when you oversalt the fries and buy more drinks, the riders who are sick when the coaster is too fast, are exactly the kind of mechanism I play these games for. I like games best when they try to mimic reality and let a thick ruleset generate stories nobody wrote, which is why I love Dwarf Fortress, and it is why I keep building simulations of my own, from a dish of neurons that learns under stimulation to a terrarium left to evolve. A chess engine, seen from that side, is the smallest simulation worth building: a complete world with rules, and inside it an agent that has to learn.

Why games, and why these three

Shannon’s point is practical. A game like chess has rules you can write down completely, a result you can read off the board without argument, and a depth that no amount of study has exhausted. That combination is rare. Most real problems have fuzzy rules, contested outcomes and no yardstick. A game gives you a laboratory where a new idea can be tested in an afternoon, against centuries of human knowledge, and the answer is a number.

Chess, shogi and Go also happen to be the three games along which the history of this field unfolded, in that order, and each one broke what had worked on the one before. That is why I picked all three rather than one.

Chess came out of northern India around the sixth century as chaturanga, travelled through Persia into Europe, and took its modern form, with the long-range queen and bishop, in Spain and Italy at the end of the fifteenth century. It is the game Shannon chose, the game Levy’s handbook teaches, and the one the classical method of search plus evaluation was built for. In 1997 IBM’s Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov by searching two hundred million positions a second on purpose-built chips, with an evaluation written and tuned by people. It was a triumph of the three parts and a disappointment to anyone hoping for insight: the machine won by looking further, not by understanding more. The interesting question, from Levy’s chapter onwards, was whether the evaluation function could be learned instead of written. For chess, that question was answered between 2018 and 2020 with a small neural network that lives inside the engine’s inner loop. It is called NNUE, and it was not invented for chess.

Shogi is the Japanese branch of the same family. It arrived in Japan by way of China and Southeast Asia by the eleventh century, took its present form by the sixteenth, and became an institution under the Tokugawa shoguns, who put the best players on stipends; the first Meijin, the title that still crowns a shogi champion, was awarded in 1612. Today it is played by millions in Japan, with a professional system, televised title matches, and a young star, Sota Fujii, who in 2023, at twenty-one, held all eight major titles at once. The board is nine by nine, each side has twenty pieces of eight kinds, and most of them promote when they reach the far third of the board. One rule makes it a different game. A captured piece changes sides, goes into the captor’s hand, and can later be dropped onto almost any empty square as a move. Nothing ever leaves the board for good, so the game never simplifies the way chess does. There are about eighty moves to choose from at a typical turn against chess’s thirty-five, the games are longer, and the endgame is a mutual race rather than a technical grind. For a programmer, drops make the evaluation function much harder to write by hand, which is why the learning happened here first. Computer shogi was transformed in 2006 by Bonanza, the first program whose evaluation was fitted to professional games rather than tuned by hand. In 2017 Ponanza beat the reigning Meijin, Amahiko Sato, and in 2018 Yu Nasu published the network design that Stockfish adopted for chess two years later. Shogi is where the idea I was chasing came from.

Go is older than both and simpler than either. It comes from China, where it is at least two and a half thousand years old and was counted among the four accomplishments of a cultivated person alongside music, calligraphy and painting; it reached Japan by the eighth century, where the Edo-period houses of professional players were funded by the shogunate, and it has deep roots in Korea, where it is called baduk. The rules fit on a card. Two players alternately place black and white stones on the intersections of a nineteen-by-nineteen grid. A group of stones with no empty points next to it is captured and removed. At the end, whoever surrounds more of the board wins, with a few points’ compensation to white for moving second. From those rules comes a game with around two hundred and fifty choices at every turn, games of two or three hundred moves, and positions that nobody has been able to score by hand. Levy’s three parts fail here. A search that looks four moves ahead in Go sees almost nothing, and there is no formula for who is winning to apply at the leaves. Go was the game that everyone in the field, including Hassabis, called the grand challenge, and it was the one DeepMind chose when it wanted to show what it had. The programs of the late 2000s had replaced the chess method with Monte Carlo tree search, which plays thousands of random games out to the end and counts who wins; that got to strong-amateur level and stuck. AlphaGo kept that search and gave it two neural networks, one to suggest moves and one to judge positions, trained first on human games and then on its own, and in March 2016 it beat Lee Sedol four games to one.

So: one game where the classical method works and the network replaces the evaluation; one where the same method strains and the network was invented; one where the method fails and the network has to guide the search itself. The three together are a short course in forty years of the field, and each one can be measured against opponents anyone can download.

Why I built it rather than read about it

Hassabis likes to cite Feynman’s line about not understanding what you cannot build, and it is the honest reason for this project. I have read the AlphaGo paper and the Stockfish NNUE write-ups more than once. I could explain the diagrams. I could not have told you what K is, or why a network that wins at equal search depth can lose at equal time, or how many hours of a laptop’s life a generation of self-play costs, because those are the things the papers leave out and the only way to learn them is to pay for them. Reading the book made the gap uncomfortable, and the same itch that makes me build terrariums wanted the world with the rules and the learner inside it running on my own machine.

The other reason is that the ingredients are, for the first time, all on my desk. The ideas are published and the reference implementations are open source. The laptop is a MacBook Pro with an Apple M4, ten cores and sixteen gigabytes of memory, which is not a research machine and has more general computing power than Deep Blue had. The browser on my phone can now run compiled code with vector instructions and real threads. And the writing of the code itself, which would have been a winter of evenings, took days with a coding agent, with me deciding what to build and the agent typing most of it. That belongs in the method: the agent wrote code, a match between two engines decided whether the code was any good, and the match does not care who wrote it.

Why Rust, and not PyTorch

The obvious way to do machine learning in 2026 is Python and PyTorch, and if the goal had been a model that answers questions on a server, that is what I would have used. The goal was an opponent on my phone, in a browser tab, offline, and that changed everything downstream.

A chess evaluation is called inside the search, about a million times a second, on one core, with no batching, rather than once per request. A network that lives there cannot be a model behind an API. It has to be a few hundred lines of arithmetic in the engine’s own language, run on integers, and updated incrementally as moves are made rather than recomputed from scratch, which is the whole trick of NNUE. The inference, in other words, had to be hand-written anyway. Once it was, the trainer was the same arithmetic run backwards, over a million parameters and inputs that are almost all zero, and it fitted in a few hundred lines too. Writing it is also how I found out what the framework would have hidden from me: the one constant I guessed instead of fitting turned a winning network into a losing one, and I would not have known why.

Rust is the language I write everything on this site in, from the neuron culture to the fantasy console, and it is the right tool for an engine for the usual reasons: no garbage collector in a loop that runs a million times a second, control over memory layout, and a compiler that produces WebAssembly with vector instructions from the same source as the native binary. One language runs from the self-play games on the laptop to the move on the phone, in one repository, and the web app has no build step. The trade-off is honest too. Training a small, sparse network on the CPU is fine. If the Go network ends up as a convolutional net with millions of dense parameters, Rust on ten cores will be slow, and I will have to decide whether to write a Metal kernel or admit that this is where the laptop study meets a GPU.

Why WebAssembly

Because the phone is the point. An opponent that lives on a server is not mine; an opponent in an app store is somebody else’s to approve. A web page that I add to my home screen, that works on a plane, and that runs the identical binary to the one on my laptop is the version I wanted, and in 2026 the browser can do it. WebAssembly has had 128-bit vector instructions for a while, and Safari now lets a page share memory between threads if it is served with the right isolation headers, so the chess engine on my phone searches on four cores. Lichess, the free chess site, runs Stockfish the same way for its analysis board, which was my proof that the approach was sound before I started.

The constraint also shaped the design more than any paper did. A network that has to be downloaded with the page and run on a phone has to be small; Kishi’s chess network is 820 kilobytes and is compiled into the engine binary. A search that has to run in a browser tab has to be frugal. Every decision that looks like taste in the code is really the phone saying no to something.

What happened

The chess engine came first: bitboards, a search with the usual family of pruning heuristics, and a hand-written evaluation borrowed from a well-known set of piece-square tables. Against Stockfish configured the way lichess configures its computer opponents, with twenty games a level on one core, it beats level 4 nineteen games to one, beats level 6 thirteen to seven, and loses to level 7 nineteen and a half to a half. If you have played the lichess computer, that places it: a solid club player, nowhere near the top.

Then the loop. The engine played itself from random openings for fifty-two minutes, which produced 5.6 million positions from fifty-seven thousand games, each labelled with what the search thought of it and how the game ended. A network trained on those positions in under twenty minutes beat the hand-written evaluation it replaced by 85 rating points, plus or minus 32, when both sides were allowed the same number of positions to look at. When both sides were allowed the same number of milliseconds, they came out even, because the network costs two and a half times as much per position. That is the whole problem of this kind of learning in one sentence, and I did not understand it before I had the numbers.

Shogi got its own engine with the same shape and a hand-written evaluation, which beats Fairy-Stockfish’s weakest setting twenty games to none and loses to a middling one eighteen to two. Go got the method of the late 2000s, Monte Carlo tree search with the shape patterns from the old MoGo program, and against GNU Go at its lowest level, with a second a move, it wins three games in ten. All three play on the phone. The chess one is the only one I would call a satisfying opponent at the top levels, and that is with the hand-written evaluation, because the trained network has not yet earned its place on the clock.

What this opened up

I started with one question, whether I could build Levy’s three parts, and I have ended the month with five better ones.

The chess network wins at equal search and draws at equal time. Does that change after more generations of self-play, as the games it learns from get stronger, or is a laptop-sized network always going to be paying for its own cost? The loop is running as I write this, at low priority, so the laptop stays usable. Why did one constant swing the result by 176 rating points, and what does that say about the contract between a learned component and the hand-tuned system it plugs into? Does the same loop work for shogi once the network can see where the kings are, which is what Nasu’s original design did and mine does not yet? Go needs the second kind of loop, where the search teaches the network which moves to look at, and I do not know what a laptop can train on a full nineteen-by-nineteen board; the AlphaGo chapters of the book, which I am about to reach, will tell me what it took in 2016, and I want to know what it takes in 2026 on a machine from a shop. And underneath all of it: how much of an engine’s strength survives the trip from a native binary to a browser tab on a phone, and what threads buy back.

Each of those is a few days of work and a few numbers, and I have started keeping a notebook in the repository so that the numbers are written down as they arrive, failures included. If the answers turn out to be as interesting as the questions, this may become the first of several pieces, one idea at a time, chess first, then shogi, then Go. Let’s see.
